name: Epristeride

angle.text: Hair-loss forum users discuss epristeride as a finasteride-like DHT blocker for keeping scalp hair. Its hair use was explored but never approved, and it is marketed in China for prostate enlargement, so the appearance use rests on its mechanism and limited data.

summary: A Chinese BPH drug of the finasteride family; hair-loss use was explored but never approved.
note: No published hair-loss trial results found; sold in China as a BPH drug.
currentQuick:
Epristeride is an oral 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor sold in China for enlarged prostate. It was tested for hair loss and acne during development but not approved for them.
The sources reviewed contain no published hair-loss trial data.
How it works: It blocks the type 2 form of 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that turns testosterone into DHT, the hormone linked to pattern hair loss.
Risks and caveats: Safety information is sparse in the sources reviewed. As a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor it is prescription-only where marketed, and it is not sold in the US, UK or Japan.
deepLead:
Epristeride is an oral steroidal 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that lowers conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). It is marketed in China for benign prostatic hyperplasia under brand names including Aipuliete and Chuanliu .
It was also investigated for male pattern hair loss and acne, but those uses were never approved, according to Wikipedia . It is therefore of interest to hair-loss communities as a finasteride-like compound, although the sources reviewed contain no hair-loss trial results.
Laboratory work describes it as a selective inhibitor of the type 2 isoform of the enzyme .

name: Alfatradiol (Ell-Cranell Alpha)

angle.text: Users apply alfatradiol, sold in Germany and Latin America, as a non-finasteride option for pattern hair loss in men and women. It has been studied for this use in trials, which describe slowed loss with little regrowth.

summary: A weak topical estrogen sold in Germany for hair loss; seems to slow loss but regrows little.
note: Not FDA approved; weaker than minoxidil in a head-to-head trial in women.
currentQuick:
Alfatradiol is a topical form of 17-alpha-estradiol, sold in Germany and parts of Latin America for pattern hair loss.
In the one randomized comparison found, 2% minoxidil outperformed it in women; reports describe it mainly as slowing loss.
How it works: It is described as inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase, lowering DHT locally in the scalp, and has weak estrogen-receptor activity.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects are mostly local itching or burning, attributed to the alcohol vehicle. Safety in pregnancy, breastfeeding and under 18 is unknown. It is not FDA approved.
deepLead:
Alfatradiol, also called 17-alpha-estradiol, is a stereoisomer of the main human estrogen, 17-beta-estradiol. It is applied to the scalp as a low-concentration ethanolic solution to treat androgenetic alopecia in men and women, and is sold in Germany and several Latin American countries under names including Ell-Cranell Alpha, Pantostin, Avixis and Avicis .
It has far weaker estrogenic activity than estradiol and is described as inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that makes DHT . It is not FDA approved .
A randomized comparison in 103 women found minoxidil outperformed alfatradiol, and Wikipedia reports that alfatradiol slowed or stabilized hair loss without increasing hair density .

name: Topilutamide (Fluridil)

angle.text: Topilutamide is a scalp antiandrogen sold in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, and users interested in topical alternatives to oral DHT blockers discuss it for pattern hair loss. It is studied for this use, though published trial data is small.

summary: A topical antiandrogen sold in the Czech Republic and Slovakia for hair loss, with little published trial data.
note: Not FDA or EMA approved; evidence limited to small older studies.
currentQuick:
Topilutamide (fluridil) is a topical antiandrogen sold as Eucapil for pattern hair loss in two European countries.
The sources reviewed describe small older studies and lab data; no large randomized trials were found.
How it works: It blocks the androgen receptor in the scalp and is reported to break down quickly in human serum.
Risks and caveats: Safety data are limited in the sources reviewed. It is not approved by the FDA or EMA for hair loss.
deepLead:
Topilutamide, also called fluridil (code BP-766), is a topical nonsteroidal antiandrogen applied to the scalp for pattern hair loss in men and women. It is marketed as a 2% product, Eucapil, by Interpharma Praha .
Wikipedia describes it as approved for cosmetic use in Europe and sold only in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, with no FDA or EMA approval for androgenetic alopecia .
Evidence is limited to preclinical receptor studies and older small clinical reports described in secondary sources; the sources reviewed give no quantitative trial results .

name: Dimethylcurcumin (ASC-J9)

angle.text: ASC-J9 is an experimental anti-androgen that has attracted interest as a topical acne approach because it reduces androgen receptor protein. It reached two Phase 2 acne trials, but no results were found, so the appearance benefit remains a theory.

summary: An experimental curcumin-derived anti-androgen that breaks down the androgen receptor; tried as an acne cream in two Phase 2 trials with no published results found.
note: Not approved anywhere; human acne trial results are not published in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
ASC-J9 (dimethylcurcumin) is an experimental, curcumin-derived compound that lowers androgen receptor levels rather than just blocking the receptor. It has been studied in labs for prostate cancer and other conditions, and as a topical cream for acne.
Two Phase 2 acne trials (2007 and 2011, around 180 participants each) are registered as completed, but no published results were found, so its effect on acne in people is unestablished.
How it works: It is described as an androgen receptor degradation enhancer: it appears to reduce the amount of AR protein in cells, which is the idea behind using it on skin where androgens contribute to acne.
Risks and caveats: It is experimental and not approved by regulators. Human safety data from the acne trials are not published in the sources reviewed; most other data come from cell and animal studies.
deepLead:
Dimethylcurcumin, known by the development code ASC-J9 (and also GO-Y025), is a synthetic curcumin derivative described as a nonsteroidal antiandrogen. Unlike conventional androgen receptor (AR) blockers, it is reported to work by promoting degradation of the androgen receptor protein rather than only occupying the receptor. It is listed as an experimental drug and is not approved for any use.
In appearance-related contexts it has been of interest as a topical anti-androgen for acne. Two Phase 2 trials of an ASC-J9 cream in acne were registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, one starting in 2007 with 186 participants and one in 2011 with 181 participants. Both are listed as completed, but no peer-reviewed results for them are among the sources reviewed for this article, so its effect on acne in humans is not established in the published literature found here.
Most published work on ASC-J9 is laboratory and animal research, led by the group of Chawnshang Chang, in areas such as prostate cancer, spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy, bladder and liver cancer models, and wound healing.

name: Drospirenone

angle.text: Drospirenone-containing contraceptive pills are used by women for clearer skin because the progestin has anti-androgen activity. The FDA labels certain drospirenone pills for moderate acne in women who also want contraception, so the acne use is studied.

summary: An antiandrogenic progestin in some contraceptive pills, FDA-labelled for moderate acne in women who also want birth control, with a debated clot-risk signal.
note: Prescription-only; boxed warning on smoking and cardiovascular events; VTE risk compared with other pills is debated.
currentQuick:
Drospirenone is a prescription progestin related to spironolactone. In the combined pill Yaz it is labelled for moderate acne in women at least 14 who also choose the pill for contraception.
Its antiandrogenic and antimineralocorticoid actions are the usual explanation for the acne benefit and for less fluid retention than some older progestins.
How it works: It activates the progesterone receptor to suppress ovulation while blocking androgen and mineralocorticoid receptors, which lowers androgen signalling in skin.
Risks and caveats: Common effects include headache, irregular bleeding, nausea, breast tenderness and mood changes. Combined pills carry a boxed warning for smokers over 35, and registry studies have reported more venous clots with drospirenone pills than with levonorgestrel pills, though the size of the difference is debated. Rarely it can raise potassium. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Drospirenone is a synthetic progestin structurally related to the diuretic spironolactone. In addition to activating the progesterone receptor, it blocks the mineralocorticoid and androgen receptors, which gives it a profile that is often described as closer to natural progesterone than that of older progestins. It is taken by mouth, most often combined with an estrogen in contraceptive pills, and also as a progestogen-only pill.
For appearance purposes its relevance is acne. A US-labelled combination of drospirenone and ethinyl estradiol (Yaz) is indicated to treat moderate acne in women at least 14 years old who also want an oral contraceptive, alongside its contraceptive and premenstrual dysphoric disorder indications. Its antiandrogenic activity is the mechanism usually cited for this effect.
Drospirenone pills carry the same boxed warning about smoking and cardiovascular events as other combined oral contraceptives, and large registry studies and a network meta-analysis have examined whether drospirenone-containing pills are associated with more venous thromboembolism than levonorgestrel pills.

name: Dienogest

angle.text: Dienogest is a progestin in some pills that are prescribed to women partly for acne, because of its anti-androgenic profile. Its acne link rests on that pharmacology and pill-level use, with no acne-specific trials in the sources reviewed.

summary: An antiandrogenic progestin used for endometriosis and in some pills that are prescribed for acne, with no acne-specific trials in the sources reviewed.
note: Prescription-only; acne use is only via combined contraceptive pills and varies by country.
currentQuick:
Dienogest is a prescription progestin best known as a standalone endometriosis treatment and as the progestin in several combined pills. Because it has antiandrogenic activity, some ethinylestradiol/dienogest pills are used or labelled for acne in women who also want contraception.
Evidence is stronger for endometriosis than for acne; no acne-specific trials were found among the sources reviewed.
How it works: It activates the progesterone receptor and blocks the androgen receptor, suppressing ovulation and reducing androgen effects such as oiliness and acne, without androgenic activity of its own.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include irregular bleeding, headache, nausea, breast tenderness, mood changes and weight gain. Combined pills carry a boxed warning for smokers over 35 and an increased clot risk; long-term use may lower bone density. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Dienogest is a synthetic progestin derived from 19-nortestosterone, developed by Bayer's predecessor companies. It is used as a 2 mg standalone treatment for endometriosis in many countries and as the progestin in several combined oral contraceptives and menopausal products. It is sometimes called a fourth-generation progestin.
Dienogest differs from many 19-nortestosterone progestins in that it is described as having antiandrogenic rather than androgenic activity, and this is the basis for its interest in acne. Wikipedia notes that acne is not a listed indication for standalone dienogest but that an estradiol valerate/dienogest product was in registration in Europe for acne, while Grokipedia states that ethinylestradiol/dienogest combinations are approved in the European Union for moderate acne in women who choose oral contraception and for whom topical treatment or antibiotics failed.
Combined products carry the standard combined-pill boxed warning about smoking and cardiovascular events.

name: Chlormadinone acetate

angle.text: Chlormadinone acetate pills, sold in parts of Europe, are used by women for acne and oily skin thanks to the progestin's anti-androgen action. Support comes from open-label studies rather than large controlled trials.

summary: An antiandrogenic progestin in some European contraceptive pills used for acne and oily skin, supported by open-label data rather than large trials.
note: Prescription-only; not marketed in the US; meningioma has been reported with prolonged high-dose progestin use.
currentQuick:
Chlormadinone acetate is a prescription progestin with antiandrogenic effects, mainly found in combined contraceptive pills (such as Belara) sold outside the US. Doctors use these pills for women with acne, oily skin or hirsutism who also want contraception.
Acne evidence in the sources reviewed comes from open-label studies; no large randomized acne trial was found.
How it works: It activates the progesterone receptor, blocks the androgen receptor and suppresses LH and FSH, lowering androgen effects in skin and hair follicles.
Risks and caveats: Low-dose pills commonly cause irregular bleeding, headache, nausea and breast tenderness. High doses have been linked to adrenal and metabolic effects, and prolonged high-dose use to meningioma. It is prescription-only and was withdrawn in the US around 1970 after dog mammary tumour findings.
deepLead:
Chlormadinone acetate (CMA) is a synthetic progestin derived from 17-hydroxyprogesterone. It has progestogenic activity together with antiandrogenic effects, acting both by blocking the androgen receptor and by lowering gonadotropin-driven hormone production. It is mostly used at 2 mg in combined oral contraceptives with ethinylestradiol (for example Belara), in some menopausal hormone therapies, and at higher doses for prostate conditions in Japan and South Korea.
In the appearance context it is used in pills prescribed to women with acne, seborrhea, hirsutism or female pattern hair loss, similarly to cyproterone acetate. Grokipedia reports open-label studies of an ethinylestradiol/CMA pill in mild to moderate papulopustular acne over 12 cycles.
It is not marketed in the United States. Reports of meningioma with prolonged high-dose use of related progestins have prompted regulatory attention in Europe.

name: Nomegestrol acetate

angle.text: Nomegestrol acetate is a European pill progestin with mild anti-androgenic activity, and some discussion links it to skin benefits for acne-prone users. That link is inferred from its pharmacology, and no acne trial was found.

summary: A mildly antiandrogenic progestin in European pills; any acne benefit is suggested by its pharmacology, with no acne trial found.
note: Prescription-only; not available in the US or Canada; meningioma risk reported with prolonged therapeutic doses.
currentQuick:
Nomegestrol acetate is a prescription progestin used with estradiol in the Zoely contraceptive pill and alone for some gynaecological conditions. It is sold in Europe and Australia but not the US.
It has mild antiandrogenic activity, so acne improvement is suggested in reference works, but no acne trials were found.
How it works: It selectively activates the progesterone receptor to suppress ovulation and has weak androgen receptor blocking activity.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects are typically mild: irregular bleeding, headache, nausea and breast tenderness. Prolonged use at therapeutic doses has been associated with meningioma in epidemiological studies. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Nomegestrol acetate (NOMAC) is a synthetic progestin derived from 19-norprogesterone. It is a potent, selective progesterone receptor agonist that suppresses ovulation and has some antiandrogenic activity, with no important androgenic, estrogenic, glucocorticoid or antimineralocorticoid effects. It is used in combination with estradiol as a contraceptive pill (Zoely), for menopausal hormone therapy, and alone for certain gynaecological conditions (Lutenyl).
In the appearance context, Wikipedia states that its antiandrogenic activity may help with acne, seborrhea and other androgen-dependent symptoms in women. No acne-specific trial was among the sources reviewed, and Grokipedia lists acne among reported side effects of the drug.
It is approved in Europe and Australia but not in the United States or Canada; the US FDA rejected the Zoely application in 2011. Prolonged use of therapeutic doses has been associated with meningioma in epidemiological studies.

name: Abiraterone acetate

angle.text: Abiraterone is a prostate-cancer drug that lowers testosterone and DHT, so it comes up in androgen-focused discussion as a theoretical route to protecting scalp hair or skin. It is not used for appearance, and no hair or skin studies were found in the sources reviewed.

summary: A prescription prostate-cancer drug that blocks androgen synthesis; no hair or skin studies exist in the sources reviewed.
note: Oncology drug with labelled risks (blood pressure, potassium, adrenal and liver effects, fetal harm); no appearance use studied.
currentQuick:
Abiraterone acetate is a prescription oral drug for advanced prostate cancer. It shuts down androgen production by inhibiting the enzyme CYP17A1.
It is discussed alongside anti-androgens for hair, but no study among the sources reviewed has tested it for hair loss or other appearance outcomes.
How it works: It blocks CYP17A1 in the testes, adrenal glands and tumours, cutting production of testosterone and related androgens; it is given with prednisone to offset the resulting hormone imbalance.
Risks and caveats: Labelled risks include high blood pressure, low potassium, fluid retention, adrenal insufficiency, liver toxicity and fetal harm. It is prescription-only and used under oncology supervision.
deepLead:
Abiraterone acetate (brand names Zytiga and Yonsa) is an oral prodrug converted in the body to abiraterone, an inhibitor of the enzyme CYP17A1, which lowers production of androgens including testosterone and DHT. It is approved for advanced prostate cancer, given with prednisone, and is a prescription cancer drug rather than a cosmetic or dermatological product.
It is included here because it is discussed in connection with anti-androgen approaches to hair. No published study among the sources reviewed has tested abiraterone for hair loss, acne or any other appearance outcome, so its effect on appearance in people is untested.
Its labelled risks include mineralocorticoid excess effects (hypertension, low potassium, fluid retention), adrenal insufficiency and liver toxicity, and its label states it can cause fetal harm.

name: Cimetidine

chain: Slightly less sebum or body hair
angle.text: Cimetidine, an acid reducer, has been tried occasionally for acne and excess hair growth in women because of weak antiandrogen activity. References describe that effect as small, and the appearance use is a side-effect-based, off-label idea.

summary: An acid-reducing H2 blocker with weak antiandrogen action that has been floated for acne and hirsutism; references describe the effect as too weak to matter.
note: Inhibits many liver enzymes and interacts with other drugs; rare gynecomastia.
currentQuick:
Cimetidine is an over-the-counter and prescription acid reducer. It has a weak antiandrogenic effect, so some have tried it for acne or excess hair in women.
Wikipedia reports that the effect is too weak to help those conditions and that such use is not recommended. No acne or hirsutism trials appear in the sources reviewed.
How it works: It blocks histamine H2 receptors in the stomach lining, and at high doses weakly blocks the androgen receptor and affects estrogen metabolism.
Risks and caveats: Usually mild side effects such as diarrhea, rash, dizziness and fatigue; rare gynecomastia or sexual dysfunction, mainly at high doses. It inhibits liver enzymes and interacts with many drugs including warfarin and theophylline.
deepLead:
Cimetidine (brand name Tagamet) is a histamine H2-receptor antagonist that reduces stomach acid, used mainly for ulcers and heartburn.  It also has weak antiandrogenic activity, which is why it has occasionally been tried for acne and excess hair growth (hirsutism) in women. 
Wikipedia states that this antiandrogenic effect is too weak to help much with acne, hirsutism or hyperandrogenism in women, and that these uses are not recommended.  No clinical studies of cimetidine for appearance conditions are summarised in the sources used here.

name: Erythromycin (acne)

angle.text: Topical erythromycin is a prescription antibiotic labelled in the US for acne, and users typically pair it with benzoyl peroxide to limit bacterial resistance. It is studied and approved for this specific appearance use.

summary: A prescription macrolide antibiotic solution for acne, usually paired with benzoyl peroxide because acne bacteria can become resistant.
note: Often combined with benzoyl peroxide to limit antibiotic resistance.
currentQuick:
Topical erythromycin 2% is a prescription antibiotic labelled in the US for acne vulgaris. Reference sources describe it as a mild-to-moderate acne option, typically combined with benzoyl peroxide.
It is a long-established antibiotic, introduced in 1952.
How it works: It binds the bacterial ribosome and stops protein synthesis, reducing acne-associated bacteria.
Risks and caveats: Local dryness, peeling, itching, redness; rare hives. Labels warn of antibiotic-associated colitis. Reference sources note it is usually paired with benzoyl peroxide to limit resistance.
deepLead:
Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that blocks bacterial protein synthesis.  A 2% topical solution is labelled in the US for the treatment of acne vulgaris. 
Acne guidance summarised in a reference encyclopedia describes topical antibiotics, including erythromycin, as typically combined with benzoyl peroxide to limit the development of antibiotic resistance.

name: Sulfacetamide

angle.text: Sulfacetamide, usually combined with sulfur, is a prescription lotion or wash used for acne, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis, giving clearer and less red skin. These uses are the product's labelled indications and are clinically studied.

summary: An old sulfa antibiotic, usually paired with sulfur in prescription lotions and washes for acne, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis.
note: Not for people allergic to sulfa drugs; rare serious skin reactions are on the label.
currentQuick:
Sodium sulfacetamide is a sulfonamide antibiotic applied to the skin, often combined with sulfur, for acne, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis.
It is a prescription product in the US, and the sources reviewed describe its role rather than citing trial results.
How it works: It blocks bacterial folic acid synthesis to slow bacterial growth; sulfur adds a keratolytic effect.
Risks and caveats: Mild stinging, dryness and irritation are most common. The US label warns of Stevens-Johnson syndrome in sulfonamide-sensitive people and reports of drug-induced lupus, including one fatal case.
deepLead:
Sulfacetamide is a sulfonamide antibiotic used on the eyes and skin.  In dermatology it is most often sold as sodium sulfacetamide, frequently combined with sulfur, for acne vulgaris, rosacea with papules and pustules, and seborrheic dermatitis. 
A review of topical acne agents and the US product label describe it as a prescription topical option; reported hypersensitivity is uncommon, but the label carries warnings about Stevens-Johnson syndrome in sulfonamide-sensitive people.  No clinical trials of it are summarised in the sources reviewed.

name: Nadifloxacin

angle.text: Nadifloxacin is a topical antibiotic cream used for acne in Japan, parts of Europe and Asia, and people elsewhere discuss it as an import option. Its main use is acne, where it has been studied in clinical settings.

summary: A topical quinolone antibiotic cream for acne used in Japan, parts of Europe and Asia but not the US.
note: Not US-approved; concern about quinolone resistance.
currentQuick:
Nadifloxacin is a 1% antibiotic cream for acne and skin infections, available in Japan, some European and Asian countries.
Small studies reportedly show lesion reductions comparable to clindamycin combinations, but evidence in the sources is limited.
How it works: It inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase, killing or stopping acne-related bacteria such as Cutibacterium acnes, and may have anti-inflammatory effects.
Risks and caveats: Mostly local burning, itching, dryness. Wikipedia notes concern that topical quinolones could promote resistance. Not approved in the US.
deepLead:
Nadifloxacin is a topical fluoroquinolone antibiotic used mainly for acne vulgaris and, secondarily, for bacterial skin infections.  It inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase. 
It is marketed as a 1% cream in Japan, parts of Europe and some Asian countries, and is not approved in the United States.  Wikipedia notes concern that topical quinolone use could promote quinolone resistance.

name: Azithromycin pulse (acne)

angle.text: Dermatologists sometimes prescribe short, intermittent azithromycin courses off-label for inflammatory acne, often when other options are not suitable. Evidence consists of small head-to-head trials.

summary: Short intermittent courses of an oral macrolide antibiotic used off-label for inflammatory acne; evidence is small head-to-head trials and resistance is a stated concern.
note: Prescription antibiotic; QT prolongation warning and antibiotic-resistance concerns.
currentQuick:
Azithromycin is a prescription macrolide antibiotic. Some prescribers use it in intermittent 'pulse' courses for inflammatory acne, often as an alternative to tetracycline-class antibiotics.
Published support consists mostly of small registered trials against doxycycline or minocycline or with add-ons such as probiotics; the registry records cited do not report outcomes.
How it works: It blocks bacterial protein synthesis and accumulates in tissues with a half-life of about 68 hours, which is why short or intermittent courses are used. The bacterial target in acne is Cutibacterium acnes.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are gastrointestinal. The FDA has warned about QT prolongation, and acne guidance cautions that repeated antibiotic exposure has increased resistant C. acnes, generally recommending courses of no more than about three months.
deepLead:
Azithromycin pulse dosing for acne refers to the use of the oral macrolide antibiotic azithromycin in short, intermittent courses (for example on a few days each week) as a treatment for inflammatory acne vulgaris. It is an off-label dermatology practice in many countries; azithromycin is a prescription-only antibiotic, and the pulse schedule is a prescriber's decision rather than a product category.
Azithromycin was discovered in 1980 by the Zagreb pharmaceutical company Pliva, approved for medical use in 1988, and launched by Pfizer as Zithromax in 1991. It binds the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and has a long tissue half-life of about 68 hours, which is the pharmacological basis for short or intermittent courses.
Evidence for the acne use consists mainly of small registered trials comparing azithromycin with doxycycline, minocycline, or add-on agents such as probiotics, levamisole or light therapy. The general acne literature notes that dermatologists prefer antibiotics in combination with non-antibiotic agents and that resistant Cutibacterium acnes strains, including to macrolides, have increased.

name: Aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy

angle.text: Clinics use ALA with light for actinic keratoses, and it is investigated for acne and skin quality, where users hope for less oil and clearer skin. The acne use is investigational, with mixed trial signals.

summary: A clinic procedure pairing topical ALA with light to treat actinic keratoses; its acne use is investigational, with mixed trial signals.
note: Clinic-only; pain, redness and photosensitivity are common; acne is not a labelled use.
currentQuick:
ALA PDT applies a heme precursor to the skin, then shines light on it so the skin's own conversion product destroys targeted cells. Its labelled dermatology uses are actinic keratosis and superficial basal cell carcinoma.
For acne it is still described as investigational: a 2016 systematic review was favourable, while one phase II trial found no advantage over blue/violet light alone.
How it works: ALA becomes protoporphyrin IX in skin cells; light activates it in the presence of oxygen, producing reactive oxygen species that damage cells.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are redness, pain or burning and photosensitivity. The label also warns of hypersensitivity, transient amnestic episodes and eye injury from the lamp; eye protection is required.
deepLead:
Aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy (ALA PDT) is a procedure in which aminolevulinic acid, a precursor of heme, is applied to the skin and the area is then illuminated with a specific light source. The skin converts ALA into protoporphyrin IX, a light-sensitive compound that produces reactive oxygen species when illuminated and damages targeted cells.
In the United States the topical ALA product Ameluz, used with a red-light lamp, is labelled for actinic keratoses on the face and scalp and for superficial basal cell carcinoma; acne is not a labelled indication. Use for acne is described as still under clinical investigation, with a 2016 systematic review calling it a safe and effective method and one phase II trial finding it not superior to blue/violet light alone.
Common side effects are application-site redness, pain and burning, and a period of photosensitivity.

name: Trichloroacetic acid (TCA peel)

chain: New skin forms in its place
Smoother texture, less pigment and scarring
angle.text: TCA peels are done by clinicians to improve skin texture, uneven pigment and acne scars, with visible skin renewal after healing. Registered trials exist for these uses, but outcomes were not reported in the records reviewed.

summary: A medium-depth chemical peel acid used by clinicians for skin texture, pigment and scars; registered trials exist but outcomes aren't reported in the records.
note: Caustic acid; burns, pigment change and scarring are possible, so it is described as a provider-performed procedure.
currentQuick:
TCA is a strong acid used as a medium-depth chemical peel and for wart removal. Clinicians use it for texture, pigment and some scars;.
Several small trials are registered for acne, melasma and scars, but the registry entries cited do not report results.
How it works: The acid causes controlled chemical injury to the skin surface, which then peels and regenerates. Depth depends on concentration and technique.
Risks and caveats: The European Chemicals Agency says it causes severe skin burns and eye damage. Deeper peels carry risks of prolonged redness, pigment change, milia, atrophy and scarring, and Wikipedia says medium peels should be done by a medical provider.
deepLead:
Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) is a strong organic acid used in dermatology as a chemical peel and as a topical agent to destroy warts. It was discovered by the French chemist Jean-Baptiste Dumas in 1839, and in laboratories is widely used to precipitate proteins and nucleic acids.
A TCA peel is classed as a medium-depth peel, which Wikipedia says should be performed by a medical provider, usually in a clinic or outpatient surgical setting; patients commonly report a warm or burning sensation. General complications of deeper peels include prolonged redness, pigment change, milia, atrophy and scarring.
Registered studies include TCA peels for acne, melasma, lentigines and atrophic varicella scars; the registry records cited here do not report outcomes. A point-wise variant known as TCA CROSS is used by clinicians for atrophic scars, but none of the sources cited here describe it.

name: Corticosteroid injection (Kenalog for cysts)

angle.text: Acne forum users describe a clinician-given triamcinolone injection as a way to shrink and calm one large inflamed pimple quickly. It is an off-label procedure, and no acne-cyst trials were found in the sources used.

summary: A clinician-injected steroid (triamcinolone) used off-label on single inflamed pimples; no acne-cyst trials were found in the sources used.
note: Prescription drug given by a clinician; no acne trials found here.
currentQuick:
Intralesional steroid injection places a small amount of a corticosteroid such as triamcinolone (Kenalog) directly into an inflamed lesion. In acne communities it is discussed as a way to reduce an individual cyst or nodule.
Triamcinolone is a well-established drug with documented dermatologic uses, including keloid and hypertrophic scars, but no study of acne cysts appears in the sources used here.
How it works: Triamcinolone is a potent glucocorticoid that reduces inflammation at the site where it is placed.
Risks and caveats: It is prescription-only. Documented effects from other injection routes include raised eye pressure and, with intravitreal use, rare endophthalmitis; systemic effects such as menstrual irregularity are listed by Wikipedia.
deepLead:
Intralesional corticosteroid injection means injecting a small amount of a corticosteroid, most often triamcinolone acetonide (brand name Kenalog), directly into a skin lesion such as an inflamed acne nodule or cyst. Acne forums describe it as a way to reduce the size and redness of an individual pimple, and it is a clinician-administered procedure.
Triamcinolone acetonide is a synthetic corticosteroid about eight times as potent as prednisone. Wikipedia lists intralesional injection for inflammation in skin lesions, notably hypertrophic and keloid scars, alongside joint, intravitreal, topical and nasal uses. It is prescription-only in the US, EU and UK.
No trial of intralesional triamcinolone for acne cysts appears among the sources used here; registered studies of intralesional triamcinolone concern alopecia areata and keloids.

name: Basil oil (acne)

angle.text: Basil oil is promoted in natural-skincare circles as a topical for acne because it shows antibacterial activity in the lab, including against the acne bacterium. The evidence is in vitro only, and no human acne studies were found.

summary: A plant essential oil with lab antibacterial activity, including against the acne bacterium in vitro; no human acne studies were found.
note: Only in vitro data; essential oils can irritate skin.
currentQuick:
Basil oil is distilled from Ocimum basilicum and rich in linalool and estragole. It is occasionally discussed as a natural acne agent.
The supporting research is laboratory work, including an in vitro test of Thai basil oils against the acne bacterium; no human acne trial was found.
How it works: In the lab, constituents such as linalool and eugenol show antimicrobial activity; how this would translate to skin has not been studied in people.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data for acne use are cited. Essential oils can irritate or sensitize skin, and basil oil has shown cytotoxicity in cell-line studies.
deepLead:
Basil oil is an essential oil steam-distilled from basil (Ocimum basilicum). European basil oil is high in linalool and methyl chavicol (estragole), roughly 3:1, with smaller amounts of 1,8-cineole, eugenol and myrcene; composition varies with cultivar.
Laboratory studies have found antibacterial and antifungal activity of basil oil, and one in vitro study tested Thai basil oils and micro-emulsions against Propionibacterium acnes (now Cutibacterium acnes), the bacterium linked to acne. No human trial of basil oil for acne appears among the sources used here.

name: Seaweed oligosaccharides

angle.text: Seaweed oligosaccharides are marketed as a complementary topical ingredient for acne-prone skin. The support is a single literature review, which also describes a zinc complex form.

summary: Brown-seaweed-derived sugars marketed as a complementary topical acne ingredient; support is one literature review.
note: Thin evidence base; trial details not available in the sources used.
currentQuick:
Seaweed oligosaccharides are short sugar chains from brown seaweed such as Laminaria digitata, proposed as a topical acne ingredient alone or as a zinc complex.
The main source is a 2013 literature review; no further trial data were found.
How it works: The review frames them as marine-derived alternatives to standard topical acne agents; detailed mechanisms are not given in the sources used.
Risks and caveats: No safety data are cited. Evidence is thin and effects on acne are not well characterized.
deepLead:
Seaweed oligosaccharides are short carbohydrate chains derived from the polysaccharide cell wall of brown seaweed, notably Laminaria digitata (oarweed), studied as a topical, marine-derived ingredient for acne. A published review also describes a seaweed oligosaccharide-zinc complex (SOZC).
The review, a 2013 article in the Journal of Cosmetic Science, presents them as a possible addition to benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics and retinoids as mainstay topical acne treatments. Beyond that review, the sources used here contain little human data.

name: Bumetanide

angle.text: Bumetanide appears in gray-market water-pill talk among people aiming for a drier, sharper facial look. It is a prescription diuretic for edema, and no study has tested it for facial puffiness.

summary: A potent prescription loop diuretic that appears in gray-market "water pill" talk; no study has tested it for facial puffiness.
note: Carries a boxed warning about profound fluid and electrolyte loss; banned in sport by WADA.
currentQuick:
Bumetanide is a loop diuretic that makes the kidneys excrete more salt and water. It is prescribed for swelling caused by heart, liver or kidney disease.
It has been added to this wiki because it is discussed as a gray-market "water pill" for rapid water-weight loss. No published study has examined it for facial depuffing or any appearance goal.
How it works: It blocks the NKCC2 sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, so less sodium and water are reabsorbed and urine output rises. Effects begin within about an hour and last around six hours.[1][2]
Risks and caveats: The US label carries a boxed warning that excessive amounts can cause profound water and electrolyte depletion and requires medical supervision. Reported effects include cramps, dizziness, low blood pressure, low potassium and, rarely, hearing loss and serious skin reactions. It is prescription-only in the US, UK and Australia and is prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency.[3][1]
deepLead:
Bumetanide is a loop diuretic, a prescription medicine that increases the amount of sodium and water the kidneys excrete. It is sold as Bumex, Burinex and, in a nasal-spray form, Enbumyst, among other names, and is used to treat edema (fluid retention) associated with heart failure, liver disease and kidney disease.
On a milligram basis it is described as roughly 40 times more potent than furosemide, with more complete and predictable oral absorption. It is listed on the World Health Organization Essential Medicines List.
In appearance-focused communities it is mentioned as a stronger water pill for temporarily reducing water retention. No published clinical study has tested bumetanide for cosmetic depuffing. Its US label states that excessive amounts can produce profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion and that careful medical supervision is required.
